XY takes a largest remaining piece $\\ell$ ($\\ell=p_1$ if $j\\ne1$, else $\\ell=p_2$), and then, moving first on $M''=M\\setminus\\{p_j,\\ell\\}$, guarantees $\\operatorname{odd}(M'')$ by induction.","witness":"COUNTEREXAMPLE: take M={10/34,9/34,8/34,7/34}. If LB takes 10/34 and XY takes 9/34, LB—not XY—moves first on M''={8/34,7/34}, taking 8/34. XY receives 7/34 from M'', not odd(M'')=8/34. Thus the asserted inductive guarantee and turn order are false.","load_bearing":"This step is the proof that XY can cap LB's claiming-phase payoff at odd(M). Without it, the claimed exact value (1+D(M))/2 and hence the reduction are not established."},"lower_bound":{"status":"written_and_valid","quote":null,"witness":null,"load_bearing":null},"upper_bound":{"status":"written_but_invalid","quote":"So the hypothesis of Lemma 4.1(b) holds, and some ordering of $P\\cup N$ has chain value $g\\le\\frac{S}{2^m-1}$.","witness":"NON-SEQUITUR: chain value was defined using decreasing order, but Lemma 4.1 proves only that some possibly different ordering has the desired residue. Order matters: for {10,9,8,7,5}, decreasing order has residue 5, whereas order 10,8,7,9,5 has residue 1. Indeed P={8,7,5}, N={10,9} satisfy sums 20 and 19 with no subset sum strictly between them, so the lemma's premises hold while the decreasing residue of P∪N is 5. No argument shows decreasing order preserves or lowers the residue.","load_bearing":"The subsequent XY strategy explicitly takes B={b_1≥⋯≥b_r} with the decreasing-order chain value supplied by Theorem 4.2.
